headline: Burnham says UK-EU 'status quo' is not good enough and sets 20 November summit

terms.meaning: The way things currently are.
A document where a party sets out what it will do if elected.

levels.headline: Burnham says UK-EU 'status quo' is not good enough and sets 20 November summit
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs on 12 October that the current relationship with Brussels is "not good enough", and said a UK-EU summit will take place on 20 November. It will focus on boosting growth and controlling illegal immigration.
Other items on the table include a food and drink agreement, linking energy systems, a deal on emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused him of "unpicking" the withdrawal agreement. Mr Burnham told the BBC it was "possible" that a referendum on rejoining the EU could appear in a future election manifesto, and he has ruled out a snap election.
Mr Burnham became the 59th Prime Minister in July, succeeding Sir Keir Starmer. A general election is not currently expected before 2029.
levels.why: The UK's ties with the EU shape trade, prices, travel and migration, and the debate is reopening ten years after the Brexit vote.

levels.headline: Burnham calls UK-EU relationship 'not good enough' ahead of 20 November summit
levels.body:
Andy Burnham told MPs on 12 October that the present arrangement with Brussels is "not good enough" and confirmed a UK-EU summit for 20 November. Growth and curbing illegal immigration will be central.
The agenda may include food and drink trade, energy links, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the Prime Minister was "unpicking" the withdrawal agreement. Mr Burnham has said a referendum on rejoining could be "possible" in a future manifesto, but has ruled out a snap election.
He took office in July after Sir Keir Starmer, and no general election is expected before 2029.
levels.why: Closer EU ties could change trade and migration, and the Conservatives are already opposing him.

levels.headline: PM says UK's current deal with the EU is not good enough
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on 12 October that the UK's current arrangement with the EU is "not good enough". He told MPs that a summit with the EU will be held on 20 November.
The talks will aim to help growth and tackle illegal immigration. Ideas under discussion include easier trade in food and drink, joining up energy systems, a deal on carbon trading and a youth exchange scheme. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said he was "unpicking" the Brexit deal.
Mr Burnham also said a vote on rejoining the EU might be put in a future manifesto. He has ruled out an early general election.
levels.why: Decisions on the EU affect trade, prices and who can live and work in the UK.

levels.headline: Burnham says UK-EU ties need to improve, summit set for 20 November
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK's relationship with the European Union is "not good enough" as it stands. He told MPs on 12 October that a summit with the EU will take place on 20 November.
He wants it to deliver growth and help to control illegal immigration. Possible topics are a food and drink deal, energy links, carbon trading and a youth scheme. Kemi Badenoch, leader of the Conservatives, accused him of undoing the withdrawal agreement.
Mr Burnham said a referendum on rejoining the EU is "possible" in a future manifesto, though he has ruled out a snap election.
levels.why: It could change how easily goods and people move between the UK and Europe.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants better ties with the EU
levels.body:
Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said on 12 October that how things are with the European Union now is "not good enough". He told MPs, the people elected to run the country, that there will be a meeting between the UK and the EU on 20 November.
He wants it to help the economy grow and to stop people crossing borders illegally. They might also talk about selling food and drink, sharing electricity links, and a scheme for young people. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said he was undoing the Brexit deal.
He also said that a vote on rejoining the EU could be included in a future plan for an election. He said there will be no early election.
levels.why: How close the UK is to the EU affects what we buy, what it costs and who can travel and work here.

levels.headline: Prime Minister wants to improve UK links with the EU
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says the way the UK works with the European Union is "not good enough". He said this to MPs on 12 October. The UK and the EU will meet on 20 November to talk.
He wants more jobs and growth, and fewer people arriving without permission. They may talk about food and drink, energy and a youth scheme. Kemi Badenoch, who leads the Conservative party, says he is undoing the deal made when the UK left the EU.
Mr Burnham said a future election plan could include a vote on rejoining the EU. He said he will not call an election early.
levels.why: These talks could change prices, trade and travel for people in the UK.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants a better deal with Europe
levels.body:
Britain left the European Union a few years ago. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says the deal we have with it is "not good enough". He said so on 12 October. The UK and the EU will meet on 20 November.
He wants to help the economy grow. He also wants to stop people coming in illegally. They might talk about food, energy and a scheme for young people. Another politician, Kemi Badenoch, says he is undoing the Brexit deal.
He said a vote on rejoining might one day be in his party's plan. But he said there will be no election soon.
levels.why: It could change what things cost and how people travel and work between countries.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants to be closer friends with Europe
levels.body:
The UK used to be part of a group of countries called the European Union. It left. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says the way we work with them is not good enough. The UK and the EU will meet on 20 November.
He wants to help the country make more money. He also wants to stop people from coming in the wrong way. They may talk about food, power lines, and a plan for young people. Another leader says he is undoing the leaving deal.
He says a vote on joining again could be a plan for later. He will not have an election soon.
levels.why: It could change what we buy and how we travel.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants to work more closely with Europe
levels.body:
The UK left the European Union a few years ago. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says the way we get on with it is not good enough. They will meet on 20 November.
He wants to help the country grow. He also wants to stop people coming in the wrong way.
Some politicians do not like this. He says there will be no early election.
levels.why: It could change what we buy and how we travel.

levels.headline: Britain's leader wants to work better with Europe
levels.body:
Our country used to be in a club with lots of other countries in Europe. It left the club. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, thinks the way we get on with the club is not good enough. They are going to meet on 20 November.
He wants to make it easier to sell things to each other, like food and drink. He wants help to stop people sneaking in. Some people do not like this, and one leader says he is breaking the old promise.
He says one day people might vote on joining again. But that will not be soon.
levels.why: It could change what is in the shops and where you can go on holiday.

headline: UK economy grows 0.1% in August, beating expectations

terms.meaning: The total value of everything a country produces in a given period.
Bonds issued by the UK government to borrow money.

levels.headline: UK economy grows 0.1% in August, beating expectations
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.1% in August, more than economists had expected, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Thursday 15 October. Production output rose by 0.8%, services showed no growth and construction fell by 0.2%.
Markets reacted at once. The pound rose about 0.4% against the US dollar, while yields on UK government bonds, known as gilts, fell across the curve as investors judged the figures a little less worrying for the public finances. The ONS also said growth in the second quarter had been revised up.
The picture is mixed. One economist quoted by CNBC pointed out that HMRC payroll data show about 95,000 fewer jobs over the first eight months of the year, even as output has grown. Growth is modest, and it arrives while energy prices and borrowing costs remain high.
levels.why: It shows the economy is still expanding slowly, which affects jobs, tax receipts and interest rates.

levels.headline: UK economy edges up 0.1% in August, ahead of forecasts
levels.body:
Output in the UK economy rose by 0.1% in August, ahead of what forecasters had predicted, according to figures from the ONS on 15 October. Factories, mines and energy producers did well, with production up 0.8%, but services were flat and construction shrank by 0.2%.
The pound gained around 0.4% against the dollar after the release, and the interest rate the government pays on its bonds, the gilt yield, dipped. Growth for the April to June quarter was also revised higher.
Economists warned that the numbers do not tell the whole story. Payroll records held by HMRC suggest roughly 95,000 fewer jobs so far this year, which sits oddly with rising output. The recovery is real but thin.
levels.why: Small gains in output matter because they shape tax income, hiring and the Bank of England's next move.

levels.headline: UK economy grew slightly in August, official figures show
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.1% in August, a little better than experts expected, the Office for National Statistics reported on 15 October. Production was up 0.8%, services did not grow at all, and building work fell by 0.2%.
Financial markets liked the news. The pound strengthened by about 0.4% against the US dollar, and the cost of government borrowing eased slightly. Growth earlier in the summer was also revised upwards.
Not everyone is cheerful. An economist told CNBC that tax records show about 95,000 fewer people in paid work over the first eight months of the year. So output is up, but fewer jobs are being counted.
levels.why: It tells us whether the economy is getting stronger, which affects pay, jobs and prices.

levels.headline: UK economy grows by 0.1% in August
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.1% in August, beating forecasts, official figures showed on Thursday. The Office for National Statistics said production rose 0.8%, services stood still and construction fell 0.2%.
The pound rose about 0.4% against the dollar and government bond yields fell. The ONS also raised its estimate of growth for the second quarter of the year.
However, data from HMRC suggest around 95,000 fewer jobs over the first eight months of 2026, a reminder that growth has not yet brought more work. The economy is moving forward, but only slowly.
levels.why: Slow growth limits how much the government and households can spend.

levels.headline: UK economy grows a little in August, better than expected
levels.body:
The UK economy, which means everything the country makes and sells, grew by 0.1% in August. That was a bit better than experts had guessed. The figures came from the Office for National Statistics on 15 October.
Factories and energy firms produced 0.8% more. Shops, banks and other services did not grow, and building work fell by 0.2%. The pound rose against the dollar, and the interest the government pays on its borrowing went down.
One expert noted that tax records show about 95,000 fewer jobs this year. So while the economy grew, work has not grown with it.
levels.why: A growing economy usually means more jobs and money, but this growth is very small.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew a little bit in August
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by a tiny amount in August, 0.1%. That is a little more than experts expected. The economy is all the things people make and sell in the country, and the official number counters said it grew.
Things made in factories went up by 0.8%. Services like shops and banks did not grow. Building work went down by 0.2%. The pound became a bit stronger against the US dollar.
Tax records also show about 95,000 fewer jobs than at the start of the year. So the economy is growing slowly, but not everyone is feeling it yet.
levels.why: It helps show whether people are likely to find work and whether prices and pay will rise.

levels.headline: UK economy grows slightly in August
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by a very small amount in August. It grew by 0.1%, which was more than experts thought. The economy means all the goods and services made in the country.
Factories made more, but shops, banks and other services did not grow. Builders did less work. The pound got a little stronger against the dollar, which makes things bought from abroad slightly cheaper.
Tax records show about 95,000 fewer jobs this year. That means the economy is growing, but only slowly, and fewer people are in paid work.
levels.why: It shows how well the country is doing with money and jobs.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew a tiny bit in August
levels.body:
The UK economy grew a tiny bit in August. The economy is all the things that people in the country make, build and sell. It grew by 0.1%. That is one tenth of one percent. Experts thought it might grow less.
Factories and energy firms made more. Shops and banks did not make more. Builders did less work. The pound, which is our money, got a little stronger against the American dollar.
There are about 95,000 fewer jobs than before. So the economy is growing slowly. Many people may not feel any change.
levels.why: When the economy grows, there can be more jobs and money for everyone.

levels.headline: The UK made a little more stuff in August
levels.body:
Every month, people count how much stuff our country makes and sells. This is called the economy. In August it grew a tiny bit. It was only a little more than the month before.
Factories made more things. Shops and banks stayed the same. Builders did less building. Our money, the pound, became a bit stronger next to American money.
Some people lost their jobs this year. About 95,000 fewer people have jobs than before. So the country is growing, but very slowly.
levels.why: It tells us if people will have enough work and money.

levels.headline: Our country made a tiny bit more in August
levels.body:
Think of the whole country as one big shop and factory. Everyone makes things and sells things. Each month, grown-ups count how much was made. In August, a little bit more was made than before.
The factories did well. The shops and banks did about the same as before. The builders did a bit less. The pound, which is the money we use, got a little stronger.
But there are fewer jobs than there were. That is a worry. The country is growing like a small plant that is only just getting taller.
levels.why: It helps show whether the grown-ups around you will have jobs and money.

headline: UK borrowing costs stay near highest since 2007 as markets price in rate rises

terms.meaning: The annual return investors get from a UK government bond; it rises when the price of the bond falls.
The interest rate set by the Bank of England, which affects loans and savings.

levels.headline: UK borrowing costs stay near highest since 2007 as markets price in rate rises
levels.body:
The yield on UK 10-year government bonds, known as gilts, stood at around 5.3% to 5.4% in mid-October, close to its highest level since 2007. One source put it at 5.38% on 15 October. Yields fell after better-than-expected August growth figures, but remain elevated.
Traders blame energy prices linked to the Iran conflict and expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates. Bank Rate is currently 3.75%, and markets are fully pricing in a rise by the end of the year. The Bank's chief economist, Huw Pill, has been sceptical of market pricing that implies four increases over the coming year.
Higher gilt yields mean it costs the government more to borrow, which adds pressure on the public finances. The Bank's next rate decision is due on 5 November.
levels.why: High gilt yields raise the government's borrowing costs and feed into mortgage and loan rates.

levels.headline: Gilt yields stay close to 2007 highs as Bank of England hike bets build
levels.body:
UK 10-year gilt yields were around 5.3% to 5.4% in mid-October, near levels last seen in 2007. They eased slightly on 15 October after stronger growth data, but the broad picture is one of expensive borrowing.
Energy prices tied to the Iran conflict are a key driver, along with bets that the Bank of England will lift Bank Rate from 3.75%. Markets are fully pricing a rise by year end. Chief economist Huw Pill has questioned the market's expectation of four rises over the next year.
The higher yields cost the Treasury more when it borrows and tighten the room it has for spending. The next Bank decision falls on 5 November.
levels.why: The cost of government debt affects taxes, spending plans and what households pay on mortgages.

levels.headline: UK government borrowing costs remain near 19-year highs
levels.body:
The interest rate on UK 10-year government bonds, called the gilt yield, was between 5.3% and 5.4% in mid-October. That is close to the highest since 2007. It dipped a little after good growth figures on 15 October.
Two things are pushing it up. Energy prices have risen because of the conflict involving Iran, and investors expect the Bank of England to raise its rate from the current 3.75%. Markets expect at least one increase by the end of the year, though the Bank's chief economist, Huw Pill, doubts there will be as many as four.
When yields are high, the government pays more to borrow, and lenders often raise mortgage rates too. The Bank next decides on 5 November.
levels.why: Higher borrowing costs for the government can lead to higher costs for families and firms.

levels.headline: UK gilt yields stay near highest since 2007
levels.body:
UK government bond yields remained near their highest since 2007 in mid-October, with the 10-year gilt at roughly 5.3% to 5.4%. They fell slightly after better growth data on 15 October.
The causes are higher energy prices linked to the Iran conflict and expectations of Bank of England rate rises. Bank Rate is 3.75%, and traders fully expect an increase before the year is out. Bank chief economist Huw Pill has doubted the market view that there will be four rises in a year.
The higher yields raise the cost of government borrowing and limit what the Treasury can afford. The next Bank decision is on 5 November.
levels.why: Government borrowing costs shape tax and spending choices and affect mortgage rates.

levels.headline: The cost of UK government borrowing is close to a 19-year high
levels.body:
When the UK government needs money, it sells bonds called gilts. Investors who buy them get paid interest, and the rate is called the yield. In mid-October the yield on 10-year gilts was about 5.3% to 5.4%, the highest in almost two decades.
Energy prices are up because of the conflict involving Iran, and many investors think the Bank of England will raise interest rates from 3.75%. When investors expect higher rates, they ask for higher yields. One Bank official thinks they may be expecting too many rises.
A high yield means the government pays more to borrow. It can also push up mortgage rates for families. The Bank will decide on rates again on 5 November.
levels.why: It affects how much the government can spend and what families pay on loans.

levels.headline: It costs the UK government a lot to borrow money right now
levels.body:
The government sometimes borrows money by selling bonds called gilts. It pays interest on them. In October the interest rate on the main type of gilt was about 5.3% to 5.4%. That is the highest for nearly twenty years.
One reason is that energy prices have gone up because of the fighting involving Iran. Another is that people think the Bank of England will make interest rates go up. The rate is now 3.75%. The Bank decides again on 5 November.
When the government pays more interest, it has less left for schools and hospitals. Banks may also charge more for mortgages, which are loans for buying a home.
levels.why: It can mean less money for public services and dearer loans for families.

levels.headline: UK government borrowing is the most expensive in years
levels.body:
Sometimes the government needs more money than it has. It borrows by selling bonds. The people who buy them are paid interest. Right now that interest is about 5.3% to 5.4% a year. That is the highest since 2007.
Energy, like oil and gas, has become more expensive because of fighting in the Middle East. People also think the Bank of England will raise its interest rate from 3.75%. This makes lenders ask for more.
If the government pays more interest, there is less money for other things. Families can pay more for home loans too. The Bank will decide on 5 November.
levels.why: It can make loans dearer and leave less money for things we all use.

levels.headline: The government has to pay more to borrow money
levels.body:
A government can borrow money, just like a person can. It does this by selling things called bonds. It has to pay extra money, called interest, to the people who buy them. Right now the interest is very high. It is the highest for almost 20 years.
Oil and gas cost more because of fighting far away. Many people also think the Bank of England will make its rate go up. So lenders ask for more money back.
When the government pays more interest, there is less left for schools and hospitals. Mortgages, the loans for homes, can cost more too.
levels.why: It can mean less money for schools and hospitals and bigger bills for families.

levels.headline: Borrowing is costly for the country
levels.body:
The government sometimes needs to borrow money. It pays extra to the people who lend it. This extra is called interest. Right now the interest is very high. It is the highest for nearly twenty years.
Oil and gas cost more because of fighting far away. People also think the Bank of England will make its interest rate go up. So lenders ask for more.
This means the government has less money left over for things like schools.
levels.why: It can leave less money for schools and make loans cost more.

levels.headline: Borrowing money is getting pricier for the country
levels.body:
Imagine you borrow some pocket money from a friend. You promise to give back a little extra. The more the friend worries, the more extra they ask for. Countries borrow too, and they pay extra called interest.
Right now our country has to pay a lot of extra. It is the most in nearly twenty years. Oil and gas cost more because of a war far away, and people think the Bank of England will raise its rate.
When the country pays more extra, there is less money to spend on things like schools. Grown-ups might pay more on loans for houses too.
levels.why: It affects how much money is left for things like schools and how much families pay for loans.

headline: Brent settles at $105.92 as attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz keep oil high

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for crude oil.
A narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which a large share of the world's oil passes.

levels.headline: Brent settles at $105.92 as attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz keep oil high
levels.body:
Brent crude for December delivery settled at $105.92 a barrel on 15 October, down 14 cents. US West Texas Intermediate futures for November rose about 3%, or $2.88, to close at $97.97, as traders assessed possible supply disruption after attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
On 14 October Brent briefly passed $107 after Iran reportedly attacked two vessels using new tactics. One report said about 9.5 million barrels a day left Hormuz in the week to Tuesday, roughly 30% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to Kpler data. Analysts said a lack of progress in US-Iran diplomacy leaves little immediate prospect of the waterway fully reopening.
Other pressures include a hurricane shut-in in the Gulf of Mexico and Houthi attacks on Saudi targets.
levels.why: Oil near $100 raises fuel and energy costs and feeds inflation around the world.

levels.headline: Oil stays above $105 as Hormuz shipping attacks continue
levels.body:
Brent crude for December delivery closed at $105.92 a barrel on 15 October, 14 cents lower. US benchmark WTI for November rose about 3% to $97.97 as traders weighed risks to supply after attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent briefly topped $107 on 14 October after Iran reportedly attacked two vessels. Kpler data suggest about 9.5 million barrels a day left Hormuz in the week to Tuesday, around 30% below the level before the Iran war. Analysts say little progress in US-Iran talks means a full reopening is unlikely soon.
A hurricane shut-in in the Gulf of Mexico and Houthi attacks on Saudi targets add to the risk.
levels.why: Expensive oil pushes up prices for petrol, flights and goods.

levels.headline: Oil prices stay high after attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz
levels.body:
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, ended 15 October at $105.92 a barrel, 14 cents down. The US benchmark, WTI, rose about 3% to $97.97. Traders were reacting to attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
On 14 October Brent briefly went above $107 after Iran reportedly attacked two vessels. Data from Kpler show that about 9.5 million barrels a day left Hormuz in the latest week. That is about 30% less than before the Iran war. Analysts say US-Iran talks have made little progress.
A hurricane in the Gulf of Mexico and attacks on Saudi targets by the Houthis also matter.
levels.why: High oil prices make it more costly to run homes, cars and businesses.

levels.headline: Oil stays above $100 as Hormuz attacks continue
levels.body:
Brent crude, the main global oil price, settled at $105.92 a barrel on 15 October. US crude, WTI, rose about 3% to $97.97. Attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz are making traders worry about supplies.
Brent briefly passed $107 on 14 October after reports that Iran attacked two vessels. About 9.5 million barrels a day left Hormuz in the past week, around 30% below the level before the Iran war, according to Kpler. Analysts say talks between the US and Iran have not made enough progress to reopen the waterway fully.
A hurricane in the Gulf of Mexico and Houthi attacks on Saudi sites add more risk.
levels.why: Oil prices affect fuel bills, transport costs and inflation.

levels.headline: Oil prices stay very high because of attacks on ships
levels.body:
Oil is bought and sold all over the world. The main price, called Brent, ended 15 October at $105.92 a barrel. A barrel is a big container of oil. In the US, the price rose about 3% to $97.97. People are worried about attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route.
On 14 October the price briefly went over $107. About 30% less oil is passing through the route than before the war with Iran. Talks between the US and Iran have not made much progress.
A storm in the Gulf of Mexico and attacks on Saudi places make it worse.
levels.why: When oil costs more, petrol and many other things can cost more too.

levels.headline: Oil costs a lot because ships are being attacked
levels.body:
Oil is the liquid used to make petrol and many other things. It is sold by the barrel. On 15 October the main oil price ended at $105.92 a barrel. That is very high. Ships have been attacked in a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz.
About one third less oil than before is getting through that route. Talks between the US and Iran have not helped much.
A storm in the Gulf of Mexico and attacks on Saudi places have made people even more worried. When people worry, prices go up.
levels.why: It can make petrol, travel and food cost more.

levels.headline: Oil is very expensive because of attacks on ships
levels.body:
Oil is used to make petrol and diesel. It is sold by the barrel. On 15 October one barrel cost $105.92. That is a lot. Ships have been attacked in a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. Lots of the world's oil goes through it.
Now about one third less oil gets through. The talks to end the fighting have not worked yet. A storm and other attacks make people more worried.
When there is less oil, it costs more.
levels.why: It can make petrol and many other things cost more.

levels.headline: Oil is costing a lot of money
levels.body:
Oil is the stuff used to make petrol for cars and lorries. It comes from far away on ships. Right now oil costs a lot. Some ships have been attacked on a narrow sea path. That makes people afraid to send oil.
When there is less oil, people pay more for it. On 15 October a barrel of oil cost about $106.
That can make petrol, flights and many things in shops cost more.
levels.why: It can make things in shops cost more.

levels.headline: Oil costs a lot because ships are attacked
levels.body:
Oil is used to make petrol. It comes on ships, and a lot of it goes through a narrow sea path called the Strait of Hormuz. Some ships there have been attacked.
On 15 October one barrel of oil cost about $106. A barrel is a big container.
When there is less oil to buy, it costs more. Then petrol and other things can cost more too.
levels.why: It can make things in shops cost more.

levels.headline: Oil is costing a lot because ships are in danger
levels.body:
Imagine there is only one road to the sweet shop, and some people are stopping the delivery lorries. Fewer sweets reach the shop. So the sweets cost more.
Oil is like that. Lots of it travels on ships through a narrow sea path. Some ships have been attacked, so less oil gets through.
Oil costs a lot now. It can make petrol and many other things cost more.
levels.why: When something is hard to get, it costs more.

headline: US 10-year yield eases to 5.19% after hitting highest since 2002, as Fed hike bets rise

terms.meaning: The return on US government bonds; it rises when bond prices fall.
One hundredth of a percentage point.

levels.headline: US 10-year yield eases to 5.19% after hitting highest since 2002, as Fed hike bets rise
levels.body:
The yield on the US 10-year Treasury note slipped more than 2 basis points to about 5.19% on 14 October, after touching its highest since April 2002 at 5.365% on 7 October. The 30-year yield reached about 5.73% that day, its highest since May 2002. Analysts cite inflation, oil prices and fiscal worries.
The Federal Reserve raised rates by a quarter point in September, to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Minutes showed officials expect another rise by the year end, without saying when. After a hot September inflation report on 14 October, futures put the chance of a rise on 28 October at about 35%, up from 22%, and above 90% for at least one more hike by the end of the year.
Stocks have moved opposite to yields lately, though the Nasdaq hit a record on 6 October.
levels.why: US yields set borrowing costs for mortgages and loans and influence markets worldwide, including the UK.

levels.headline: US bond yields ease from 2002 highs as traders bet on another Fed rise
levels.body:
The US 10-year Treasury yield fell to about 5.19% on 14 October, down from 5.365% on 7 October, its highest since April 2002. The 30-year touched about 5.73% on the same day. Inflation, oil prices and fiscal worries are blamed.
The Fed lifted rates by 25 basis points in September to 3.75% to 4%. Minutes said another rise is expected by year end. After hot inflation figures on 14 October, the chance of a hike on 28 October rose to about 35% from 22%, and traders see over 90% odds of at least one more rise this year.
Stocks have tended to rise when yields fall, and the Nasdaq reached a record on 6 October.
levels.why: Higher US rates affect global borrowing costs and the value of the dollar.

levels.headline: US government borrowing costs ease from 24-year highs
levels.body:
The yield on the US 10-year Treasury, the return on government bonds, fell to around 5.19% on 14 October. A week earlier, on 7 October, it reached 5.365%, its highest since 2002. Worries over inflation, oil prices and government finances are behind the rise.
The Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Officials expect another rise by year end. A hot inflation report on 14 October made traders think a rise on 28 October is more likely, at about a one in three chance.
Share prices have generally moved in the opposite direction to yields.
levels.why: These yields feed through to the cost of mortgages and loans in the US and abroad.

levels.headline: US bond yields ease from highest levels since 2002
levels.body:
The US 10-year bond yield fell to about 5.19% on 14 October. It had hit 5.365% a week earlier, the highest since 2002. Higher inflation, oil prices and government borrowing worries were behind the rise.
The Federal Reserve raised rates in September to 3.75% to 4% and expects another rise by the end of the year. After a hot inflation report on 14 October, traders put the chance of a rise on 28 October at about 35%.
Stocks have tended to move the other way to yields, though the Nasdaq hit a record high on 6 October.
levels.why: US rates influence borrowing costs around the world.

levels.headline: US government borrowing costs ease after hitting a 24-year high
levels.body:
The US government borrows by selling bonds. The yield is the interest rate on them. The 10-year yield dropped to about 5.19% on 14 October. A week earlier it was 5.365%, the highest since 2002. This is because of worries about prices rising, oil costs and government debt.
The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, put up interest rates in September to between 3.75% and 4%. It expects to do it again by the end of the year. A report on 14 October showed prices rising fast, so traders think a rise on 28 October is more likely.
Share prices have mostly moved the opposite way to yields.
levels.why: What happens to US interest rates can affect the cost of loans everywhere.

levels.headline: US borrowing costs fall a little from a very high level
levels.body:
The US government borrows money by selling bonds. It pays interest on them. The interest rate went very high this month. It was the highest for over twenty years. On 14 October it came down a little, to about 5.19%.
Prices in the US are going up fast. Oil is dear too. The Fed, which is the US bank for banks, raised its main interest rate in September. It thinks it will have to raise it again before the year ends.
When interest rates are high, loans cost more.
levels.why: It affects what people pay on loans, and it matters worldwide.

levels.headline: US government pays more to borrow, but it eased a little
levels.body:
The US government borrows money by selling bonds. It pays interest on them. This month the interest rate was the highest since 2002. On 14 October it eased a little.
Prices in the US are going up. Oil costs more. The US central bank, called the Fed, raised its main interest rate in September. It thinks it may raise it again before the end of the year.
When interest rates are high, loans for homes and cars cost more.
levels.why: It makes loans dearer and affects countries all over the world.

levels.headline: The US has to pay more interest on borrowed money
levels.body:
The US government borrows money. When you borrow, you pay a bit extra back. This is called interest. This month the extra went up to the highest in more than twenty years. Then it came down a little.
The people in charge of the money, called the Fed, made interest rates higher in September. They may do it again.
High interest means loans cost more. This can be hard for people who have borrowed money.
levels.why: It makes borrowing money cost more.

levels.headline: It costs more for the US to borrow
levels.body:
The US government borrows money. It pays interest, which is extra money, to the people who lend it. This month the interest was the highest in over twenty years. On 14 October it came down a little.
Prices in the US are rising. The US central bank, the Fed, raised its main interest rate in September. It may do so again.
High interest means loans cost more.
levels.why: It makes loans cost more around the world.

levels.headline: Borrowing money costs more in the US
levels.body:
Imagine you borrow £10 from a friend, and you promise to pay back £11. The extra £1 is the interest. In the US, interest on borrowed money has gone up a lot. It is the highest in more than twenty years.
A little while ago, it went down a bit. But the people in charge may raise it again.
When the extra is bigger, borrowing is harder.
levels.why: When borrowing costs more, people and countries have less money to spend.

headline: Zelenskyy asks EU leaders for 70 billion euros in extra support at Brussels summit

terms.meaning: Money belonging to another country's bank or government that has been blocked from use.
Penalties, usually economic, imposed on a country or group.

levels.headline: Zelenskyy asks EU leaders for 70 billion euros in extra support at Brussels summit
levels.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked EU leaders on 16 October for 70 billion euros in extra support for 2027, on top of an existing 90 billion euro loan. The request is far above what Brussels has projected.
Several leaders pushed to use frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine. Denmark's prime minister called it one of the best solutions available, and Ukraine's European allies reportedly rebuffed a US plan to release a share of those assets. Talks on the next seven-year EU budget have reached an impasse.
In recent days the EU has transferred 6 billion euros to Kyiv and sanctioned nearly 1,600 individuals and entities linked to Russia's war. The European Commission is also set to confirm a 3.7 billion euro payment after Ukraine passed reforms.
levels.why: How Europe funds Ukraine will shape the war's course and the EU's own budget.

levels.headline: EU leaders weigh Zelenskyy's request for 70 billion euros more
levels.body:
At a summit in Brussels on 16 October, Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked EU leaders for an extra 70 billion euros in 2027, in addition to a 90 billion euro loan already agreed. The sum is well above Brussels' own estimates.
Leaders discussed using frozen Russian central bank assets. Denmark's prime minister described it as one of the best solutions, while Ukraine's European allies reportedly turned down a US plan to release part of the assets. The long-term EU budget talks are stuck.
The EU recently sent 6 billion euros to Kyiv and sanctioned almost 1,600 individuals and entities. A 3.7 billion euro payment is due to be confirmed after Ukrainian reforms.
levels.why: Europe is being asked to carry more of the cost of supporting Ukraine.

levels.headline: Zelenskyy asks EU for 70 billion euros more in support
levels.body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked EU leaders at a summit in Brussels on 16 October for another 70 billion euros of help for 2027. The EU has already agreed a 90 billion euro loan. The new request is more than Brussels expected.
Some leaders want to use Russian money that was frozen in Europe. Denmark's prime minister called this one of the best ideas. Ukraine's European allies reportedly turned down a US plan to release some of that money. Talks on the EU's seven-year budget are stuck.
In recent days the EU sent 6 billion euros to Kyiv and put sanctions on almost 1,600 people and groups.
levels.why: The decision affects Ukraine's war effort and what EU countries must pay.

levels.headline: Zelenskyy asks Europe for 70 billion euros more
levels.body:
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, asked EU leaders on 16 October for 70 billion euros more in 2027. This is on top of a 90 billion euro loan. The EU has not planned for anything this large.
Several leaders want to use frozen Russian central bank money to help. Ukraine's European allies reportedly rejected a US plan to release part of it. The EU is also stuck on its next seven-year budget.
The EU has just sent 6 billion euros to Kyiv and punished nearly 1,600 people and groups linked to Russia's war.
levels.why: Who pays for Ukraine's defence is one of Europe's biggest questions.

levels.headline: Ukraine's president asks the EU for a lot more money
levels.body:
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, asked leaders of the European Union for 70 billion euros more for 2027. They met in Brussels on 16 October. The EU had already agreed to lend Ukraine 90 billion euros. A euro is the money many European countries use.
Some leaders want to use Russian money that was frozen, which means locked so it cannot be spent. Others disagree about how to do it. The EU also cannot agree yet on its main budget for the next seven years.
The EU did send Ukraine 6 billion euros recently, and it put penalties on nearly 1,600 people and groups linked to the war.
levels.why: It decides how much help Ukraine gets and how much money European countries spend.

levels.headline: Ukraine asks the EU for much more money
levels.body:
Ukraine's leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, asked European Union leaders for a lot more money. He asked for 70 billion euros for 2027. They met in Brussels on 16 October. The EU already agreed to lend Ukraine 90 billion euros.
Some leaders want to use Russian money that has been frozen. Frozen means locked up so no one can spend it. The EU cannot yet agree on all its money plans for the next seven years.
Recently, the EU sent Ukraine 6 billion euros. It also punished nearly 1,600 people and groups linked to Russia's war.
levels.why: It affects how much help Ukraine gets in the war.

levels.headline: Ukraine's leader asks Europe for more money to help in the war
levels.body:
Ukraine is a country that has been fighting a war. Its leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, asked other European leaders for more money. They met in Brussels on 16 October. He asked for 70 billion euros. They had already agreed to lend 90 billion.
Some leaders want to use Russian money that was locked up in Europe. They cannot all agree how to do it. They also cannot agree yet on a big money plan for the next seven years.
Recently Europe sent Ukraine 6 billion euros to help.
levels.why: It decides how much help Ukraine can get.

levels.headline: A country in a war asks its neighbours for money
levels.body:
Ukraine is a country in a war. Its leader asked other countries in Europe for more money. They met in a city called Brussels. He asked for a very big amount.
The other countries had already given a lot. Some of them want to use money that belongs to the country that started the war, which was locked up. Not everyone agrees yet.
They are still talking about what to do.
levels.why: Countries working together can help people who are in trouble.

levels.headline: Ukraine asks Europe for more help
levels.body:
Ukraine is a country in a war. Its leader asked other European leaders for more money. They met on 16 October. He asked for 70 billion euros. A euro is the money used in lots of European countries.
They had already agreed to lend 90 billion euros. Some leaders want to use Russian money that was locked up. Not everyone agrees yet.
They are still talking.
levels.why: It decides how much help Ukraine can get.

levels.headline: Asking friends for help
levels.body:
Imagine your friend's house has a big problem and they need help. They ask all their friends for money to fix it. The friends have already given some. Now your friend asks for even more.
That is a bit like what happened in Europe. A country called Ukraine is in a war. Its leader asked its friends for lots more money.
The friends are talking about how much they can give, and how.
levels.why: Friends can help each other when things go wrong.

headline: EU leaders criticise US-Russia diesel deal as Kallas says Moscow 'miscalculated'

terms.meaning: A pause in attacks on energy sites such as refineries and power plants.
Penalties, usually economic, imposed on a country.

levels.headline: EU leaders criticise US-Russia diesel deal as Kallas says Moscow 'miscalculated'
levels.body:
EU leaders criticised a US-Russia arrangement under which Russia would supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, alongside an "energy ceasefire" between the two sides. The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told Euronews that Russia had miscalculated by trying to force Ukraine to yield through a deal with the US alone, sidelining Europe.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU will not lift sanctions on Russia until the war ends. Moscow has rejected the idea of an energy ceasefire. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he feels betrayed by Donald Trump, and there are reports of fears that the US could limit weapons sales and intelligence sharing over Ukraine's refinery strikes, which Mr Trump called a "disgrace".
Russia launched around 1,000 drones against Ukraine in a single day, Mr Zelenskyy said, and CNN reported that Ukraine has run out of Patriot interceptor missiles.
levels.why: A split between the US and Europe over Russia could change the course of the war and the sanctions on Moscow.

levels.headline: Europe pushes back on US-Russia diesel deal
levels.body:
EU leaders criticised a deal announced by the US for Russia to supply over 300,000 tonnes of diesel, together with an "energy ceasefire". Kaja Kallas told Euronews that Russia had miscalculated by sidelining Europe in talks with the US.
Ursula von der Leyen said EU sanctions on Russia will stay until the war ends. Moscow has rejected an energy ceasefire. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he feels betrayed by Donald Trump, with reports of concern that the US may cut weapons sales and intelligence sharing after Ukraine's refinery strikes, which Mr Trump called a "disgrace".
Mr Zelenskyy said Russia sent about 1,000 drones in one day. CNN reported Ukraine has run out of Patriot interceptors.
levels.why: It exposes a rift between Washington and Europe at a critical moment in the war.

levels.headline: EU criticises US-Russia diesel deal
levels.body:
EU leaders have criticised a US deal for Russia to supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, with an "energy ceasefire" between the two sides. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russia had made a mistake by leaving Europe out of talks with the US.
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said sanctions stay until the war ends. Russia has turned down the energy ceasefire. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he feels betrayed by Donald Trump. There are reports that the US could cut weapons sales and intelligence sharing because of Ukrainian strikes on refineries, which Mr Trump called a "disgrace".
Mr Zelenskyy said Russia fired about 1,000 drones in one day.
levels.why: It shows that the US and Europe disagree about how to deal with Russia.

levels.headline: EU leaders criticise US-Russia diesel deal
levels.body:
EU leaders criticised a US deal for Russia to supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, plus an "energy ceasefire". Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, said Russia had miscalculated by shutting Europe out of talks with the US.
Ursula von der Leyen said the EU will keep sanctions on Russia until the war ends. Moscow rejected the energy ceasefire. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by Donald Trump. There are reports the US may cut weapons sales and intelligence sharing over Ukraine's attacks on refineries, which Mr Trump called a "disgrace".
Ukraine says it faced about 1,000 Russian drones in a day.
levels.why: A split between allies could weaken support for Ukraine.

levels.headline: European leaders are unhappy with a US deal with Russia
levels.body:
The United States made a deal for Russia to supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel. It also announced an "energy ceasefire", which is a pause in attacks on places that make fuel and power. European leaders were unhappy. They felt Europe had been left out.
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Russia had made a mistake. The head of the EU Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said sanctions, which are penalties on Russia, will stay until the war ends. Russia said no to the pause.
Ukraine's president said he felt let down by US President Donald Trump. He said Russia sent about 1,000 drones in one day.
levels.why: It shows that countries on the same side can disagree about a war.

levels.headline: Europe is unhappy with a US and Russia fuel deal
levels.body:
The United States agreed a deal for Russia to supply a lot of diesel fuel. It also talked about a pause in attacks on fuel and power sites. European leaders were unhappy because they were not part of the talks.
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Russia had made a mistake. The EU said it will keep its penalties on Russia until the war ends. Russia said no to the pause.
Ukraine's president felt let down by the US president. He said Russia sent about 1,000 drones in one day.
levels.why: Friends who disagree can make a war harder to end.

levels.headline: Europe is cross about a deal between the US and Russia
levels.body:
The United States said Russia can sell it lots of diesel fuel. The US also talked about stopping attacks on fuel places in the war. Leaders in Europe were cross. They had not been asked.
The EU said it will keep its punishments on Russia until the war is over. Russia said it does not want the pause.
Ukraine's leader said he felt let down by the US leader. Russia sent about 1,000 drones to Ukraine in one day.
levels.why: Allies need to agree to help end a war.

levels.headline: Friends disagree about how to deal with a war
levels.body:
There is a war in Europe. Some countries are on one side and some are on the other. The United States made a deal with Russia about fuel. Europe was not asked and felt left out.
Europe said it would keep its punishments on Russia until the war is over. Ukraine's leader felt let down by the US.
It is like three friends disagreeing about how to solve a big argument.
levels.why: When friends disagree, solving a problem can take longer.

levels.headline: Europe is cross about a US deal with Russia
levels.body:
The United States made a deal for Russia to sell it lots of diesel fuel. Europe was not asked and felt left out.
Europe said its penalties on Russia will stay until the war ends. Russia said no to a pause in attacks on fuel places.
Ukraine's leader said he felt let down by the US president.
levels.why: Allies need to agree to help end a war.

levels.headline: Friends who do not agree
levels.body:
Imagine a group of friends who all want to help someone. But one friend makes a plan without asking the others. The others feel left out and a bit cross.
That is what happened with some big countries. They are all trying to deal with a war. One country made a plan without the others.
Now they have to talk it through, so they can all help in the same way.
levels.why: Friends need to listen to each other to solve big problems.

headline: Burnham meets Merz in Berlin as UK and Germany back partnership against sabotage and cyber attacks

terms.meaning: Hostile acts short of open war, such as sabotage and cyber attacks.
A formal written agreement between countries.

levels.headline: Burnham meets Merz in Berlin as UK and Germany back partnership against sabotage and cyber attacks
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin on 8 October, on his first visit to Germany as Prime Minister. Russian threats and ties with the EU were at the top of the agenda.
The two countries committed to a partnership to counter hybrid threats, meaning hostile activity such as sabotage and cyber attacks. The two leaders were also expected to formally sign off on the Kensington Treaty, a UK-Germany agreement.
The visit sits alongside Mr Burnham's wider effort to rebuild links with European partners, which includes a UK-EU summit planned for 20 November. Both governments have said they want to work more closely on security.
levels.why: Sabotage and cyber attacks can disrupt energy, transport and banking, so allies are pooling their defences.

levels.headline: UK and Germany launch partnership to counter sabotage and cyber attacks
levels.body:
Andy Burnham visited Berlin on 8 October for talks with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, his first trip to Germany as Prime Minister. Russian threats and relations with the EU were the main topics.
The UK and Germany agreed a partnership to counter hybrid threats, such as sabotage and cyber attacks. The leaders were also expected to sign off on the Kensington Treaty between the two countries.
The trip fits with Mr Burnham's push for closer links with Europe, ahead of a UK-EU summit on 20 November.
levels.why: Closer security cooperation could make both countries harder targets for hostile states.

levels.headline: UK and Germany team up against sabotage and cyber attacks
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham went to Berlin on 8 October to meet German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. It was his first visit to Germany as Prime Minister. They discussed threats from Russia and the UK's ties with the EU.
The two countries agreed to work together against hybrid threats. These are hostile acts that fall short of open war, such as sabotage and computer attacks. The leaders were also expected to sign the Kensington Treaty, a formal agreement between them.
The visit comes as Mr Burnham tries to rebuild closer links with Europe.
levels.why: Working together makes it easier to spot and stop attacks on key services.

levels.headline: Burnham and Merz agree to work together on sabotage and cyber threats
levels.body:
Andy Burnham met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin on 8 October. It was the Prime Minister's first visit to Germany in the job. Threats from Russia and the UK's relationship with the EU were top of the list.
The UK and Germany agreed a partnership to deal with hybrid threats, which means things like sabotage and cyber attacks. The two leaders were also expected to approve the Kensington Treaty.
The talks are part of a wider UK effort to strengthen ties across Europe.
levels.why: It could help protect services like power, transport and banks from attack.

levels.headline: The UK and Germany promise to work together to stop sabotage and cyber attacks
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, visited Berlin on 8 October. He met the German leader, Friedrich Merz. It was the first time Mr Burnham had visited Germany as Prime Minister. They talked about threats from Russia.
The two countries agreed to work together against sneaky attacks. These include damaging important equipment and attacking computer systems. This kind of attack is called a hybrid threat. The leaders were also expected to sign a treaty, which is a written promise between countries.
This is part of Mr Burnham's plan to be closer to other European countries.
levels.why: Attacks on power, trains or banks could affect everyone, so countries are teaming up.

levels.headline: UK and Germany team up to stop sneaky attacks
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, went to Berlin on 8 October. He met Friedrich Merz, the leader of Germany. They talked about dangers from Russia.
They agreed that the two countries will work together. They want to stop sneaky attacks like breaking important equipment and attacking computers. Leaders were also expected to sign a treaty. A treaty is a written promise between countries.
Mr Burnham also wants to be closer to other countries in Europe.
levels.why: Attacks on things like power and computers could hurt many people.

levels.headline: The UK and Germany will work together to stay safe
levels.body:
The Prime Minister of the UK, Andy Burnham, went to Germany on 8 October. He met the leader there, Friedrich Merz. They talked about danger from Russia.
They agreed to team up. They want to stop people who break important machines or attack computers. A promise between countries, written down, is called a treaty. They were expected to sign one.
The UK wants to be better friends with its neighbours in Europe.
levels.why: It helps keep important things like power and computers safe.

levels.headline: The UK and Germany will team up against bad attacks
levels.body:
On 8 October the UK leader, Andy Burnham, visited Germany. He met the German leader. They talked about people who want to cause harm.
Some people try to break important things, like power lines. Some try to attack computers. The two countries agreed to work together to stop this. Leaders also sign treaties. A treaty is a promise written on paper.
It is like two schools agreeing to look out for each other.
levels.why: Working together helps keep important things like lights and computers working.

levels.headline: The UK and Germany promise to help each other stay safe
levels.body:
The leader of the UK went to Germany on 8 October. He talked to the leader there. They talked about dangers from Russia.
Some people try to break important things or attack computers. The two countries promised to work together to stop them. They also planned to sign a treaty. A treaty is a promise written on paper.
The UK wants to be closer to its neighbours.
levels.why: It helps keep power and computers safe.

levels.headline: Two countries promise to look after each other
levels.body:
The leader of our country went to visit the leader of Germany. Germany is another country in Europe. They had a big talk.
Some people try to break things or cause trouble from far away, using computers. The two leaders said their countries will help each other stop it.
It is like when you and a friend promise to look out for each other in the playground. Together you are stronger.
levels.why: Friends who help each other can keep everyone safer.

headline: Burnham says Iran 'played a part' in September incident at RAF Fairford

terms.meaning: A branch of Iran's armed forces that answers directly to its supreme leader.
A military site where aircraft are kept and operated.

levels.headline: Burnham says Iran 'played a part' in September incident at RAF Fairford
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran "played a part" in an incident at a British air base in September. He added that it was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps, according to CNBC's report published on 1 October. The base involved is RAF Fairford.
Iran's foreign minister dismissed the claim. The accusation adds to tension in a region already under strain from the conflict involving Iran and the United States and from attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Mr Burnham became Prime Minister in July. Since then he has said he would be prepared to criticise US President Donald Trump where he disagreed, while stressing the UK's commitment to allies.
levels.why: A hostile state targeting a UK base would be a serious security issue and could shape UK foreign policy.

levels.headline: Burnham links Iran to September incident at UK air base
levels.body:
Andy Burnham has said Iran "played a part" in a September incident at a British air base, RAF Fairford. He said it was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps, CNBC reported on 1 October.
Iran's foreign minister dismissed the accusation. The claim comes as tensions rise over the conflict involving Iran and the United States and attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Prime Minister took office in July, and has said he would be willing to call out Donald Trump when he disagrees with him.
levels.why: It raises the stakes for UK security and for relations with Iran.

levels.headline: Burnham says Iran was behind a September incident at a UK air base
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on 1 October that Iran "played a part" in an incident at RAF Fairford, a British air base, in September. He said it was "almost certainly directed" by the Revolutionary Guard Corps, a branch of Iran's armed forces.
Iran's foreign minister rejected the claim. The accusation comes while tensions are already high in the Middle East, with the conflict involving Iran and the US and attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz.
Mr Burnham has been Prime Minister since July.
levels.why: It shows that Middle East tensions are affecting the UK's own security.

levels.headline: PM says Iran 'almost certainly' directed incident at RAF Fairford
levels.body:
Andy Burnham has said Iran "played a part" in a September incident at RAF Fairford, a British air base. He said it was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Iran's foreign minister denied it. The claim came as tension grew over the conflict involving Iran and the United States, and over attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Mr Burnham became Prime Minister in July. He has said he is ready to criticise Donald Trump when he thinks it is right to do so.
levels.why: A possible attack on a UK site by a foreign state is a major security matter.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says Iran was involved in an incident at a UK air base
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said Iran took part in an incident at a British air base called RAF Fairford in September. He said it was "almost certainly" planned by a part of Iran's army called the Revolutionary Guard Corps. An air base is a place where military planes are kept.
Iran's foreign minister said this is not true. The claim comes at a time of great tension in the Middle East. There is fighting involving Iran and the United States, and ships near a narrow sea route have been attacked.
Mr Burnham became Prime Minister in July.
levels.why: It could affect how safe the UK is and how it deals with Iran.

levels.headline: PM says Iran was behind an incident at a UK air base
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says Iran was involved in something that happened at a UK air base in September. The base is called RAF Fairford. Planes are kept at an air base. He said a part of the Iranian army, the Revolutionary Guard, almost certainly gave the orders.
Iran says this is not true. There is a lot of worry in the Middle East right now. There is fighting that involves Iran and the United States. Ships near a narrow sea route have been attacked.
Mr Burnham became Prime Minister in July.
levels.why: It could change how the UK deals with Iran and keeps its bases safe.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says Iran was involved at a UK air base
levels.body:
The Prime Minister is called Andy Burnham. He says that in September something bad happened at a UK air base called RAF Fairford. An air base is a place where army planes are kept. He says Iran was almost certainly behind it.
Iran says it was not. There is lots of trouble in the Middle East right now, where there is fighting and ships have been attacked.
Mr Burnham has been Prime Minister since July.
levels.why: It could change how the UK keeps its bases safe.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister blames Iran for trouble at an air base
levels.body:
Something bad happened at a place in England where army planes are kept. It is called an air base. This was in September. Our Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says he thinks the country of Iran helped to make it happen.
Iran says it did not. Iran and some other countries are already in a big argument.
The Prime Minister is like the person in charge of the whole country. He wants to keep everyone safe.
levels.why: Grown-ups in charge need to keep the country safe.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says Iran caused trouble at an air base
levels.body:
Something bad happened in September at a place where army planes are kept. It is called RAF Fairford. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says Iran almost certainly gave the orders.
Iran says this is not true. There is a lot of trouble in the Middle East right now.
The Prime Minister is the person in charge of the country. He wants to keep people safe.
levels.why: It matters because leaders want to keep the country safe.

levels.headline: The grown-up in charge says another country caused trouble
levels.body:
Something bad happened at a place where army planes stay. The person in charge of our country says a different country called Iran helped to cause it. Iran says it did not.
It is a bit like in the playground, when someone says a child from another class broke a toy, and the other child says no, it was not me.
The grown-ups must work out what is true.
levels.why: It is important to find out what really happened and keep people safe.

headline: China's exports and imports surge past expectations in September as US-China tariff cuts loom

terms.meaning: A tax charged on goods imported from another country.
A temporary agreement to hold off new trade penalties.

levels.headline: China's exports and imports surge past expectations in September as US-China tariff cuts loom
levels.body:
China's exports and imports both rose by more than economists had expected in September, according to figures reported by CNBC on 14 October. The data show the world's second-largest economy continuing to trade strongly despite US tariffs.
Washington and Beijing have each named about $30 billion worth of goods for possible tariff cuts, $60 billion in total, though neither side has said how deep the cuts will be or when they would apply. They have also extended a broader trade truce by two months, to January. It had been due to expire on 10 November.
Separately, the EU is pressing China to rebalance trade, with the European Commission hoping for tangible results by October. Analysts doubt major concessions are likely.
levels.why: China's trade with the world affects prices, jobs and the global economy, including UK shop prices.

levels.headline: China's trade beats forecasts in September while US and China plan tariff cuts
levels.body:
Both exports and imports in China rose faster than economists forecast in September, CNBC reported on 14 October. China's trade remains strong even with US tariffs in place.
The US and China have each listed about $30 billion of goods for possible tariff cuts. How deep the cuts will be, and when, is not yet known. They also extended their trade truce by two months to January, having earlier faced a 10 November deadline.
The EU, meanwhile, is pushing China to balance trade better, but analysts do not expect major concessions.
levels.why: Trade tensions between big economies can change prices and supply chains for everyone.

levels.headline: China's exports and imports grow faster than expected
levels.body:
China sold and bought more goods than economists expected in September, CNBC reported on 14 October. The figures suggest that China's trade is staying strong despite tariffs from the US.
The US and China have each named about $30 billion of goods where taxes on imports might be cut. Neither has said by how much or when. They also agreed to pause their trade dispute for two more months, until January.
The European Union is also asking China to trade more fairly, but experts do not expect China to give much ground.
levels.why: It shows how much the world's economies depend on each other.

levels.headline: China's trade grows faster than forecast in September
levels.body:
China's exports and imports both grew by more than expected in September, CNBC reported on 14 October. China's trade is staying strong despite US tariffs.
The US and China have each named about $30 billion of goods for possible tariff cuts. They have not said how deep the cuts will be or when they would start. Their trade truce has been extended by two months to January.
The EU is pressing China to balance trade, but analysts doubt China will make major concessions.
levels.why: Trade between big economies affects prices and jobs worldwide.

levels.headline: China sold and bought more than expected in September
levels.body:
China is a huge country that sells many things to the world, like phones, clothes and machines. In September it sold and bought more than experts had guessed. This was reported on 14 October.
The US charges taxes on goods from China, called tariffs. The US and China have each picked about $30 billion worth of goods where they might lower these taxes. They have not said by how much. They also agreed to pause their argument until January.
The European Union wants China to trade more fairly too.
levels.why: Trade between countries affects the prices of things in our shops.

levels.headline: China traded more than expected in September
levels.body:
China is a very big country. It makes many things that other countries buy, like toys and phones. In September, it sold more and bought more than experts thought.
The US puts extra taxes on things from China. These are called tariffs. The two countries want to make some of those taxes smaller. They have not said when. They have also agreed to stop arguing about trade until January.
Europe also wants China to trade fairly.
levels.why: It affects what things cost in the shops.

levels.headline: China sold and bought more than experts thought
levels.body:
China is a big country that makes lots of things, like phones and toys. Other countries buy them. In September China sold and bought more than people thought it would.
The US makes people pay extra taxes on things from China. The US and China might make some of these taxes smaller. They have not said when.
They have also agreed to pause their trade argument until January.
levels.why: It affects the prices of things we buy.

levels.headline: China made and sold lots of things
levels.body:
A big country called China makes lots of things. Many of the toys and phones in shops come from there. In September it sold more things than people thought it would.
Some countries put an extra tax on things from China. Now the US and China want to make the tax smaller on some things.
They are being friendlier for now.
levels.why: It can change what things cost in shops.

levels.headline: China traded more than people thought
levels.body:
China makes lots of things, like toys and phones, that other countries buy. In September it sold and bought more than people thought it would.
The US puts an extra tax, called a tariff, on things from China. The two countries want to lower the tax on some things. They have agreed to pause their trade argument until January.
Europe also wants China to trade fairly.
levels.why: It can change what things cost in shops.

levels.headline: Two countries try to be friendlier about trade
levels.body:
Think of a school fair where children swap things. Two children had an argument about swaps and now charge each other extra. It made everyone's swaps harder.
Two big countries, China and the US, did something like that with taxes on things they sell to each other. Now they want to be friendlier and lower some of the taxes.
They have said they will stop arguing for a while.
levels.why: When friends stop arguing, things can get cheaper for everyone.

headline: UK inflation figures for September due on 21 October after August rate of 3.1%

terms.meaning: Consumer Prices Index, the main measure of how fast prices are rising.
Inflation excluding food, energy, alcohol and tobacco.

levels.headline: UK inflation figures for September due on 21 October after August rate of 3.1%
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics will publish UK inflation figures for September on 21 October at 7am. The latest published figure, for August, showed consumer price inflation (CPI) at 3.1%, with the broader CPIH measure at 3.3% and RPI at 3.4%.
Core CPI, which leaves out food, energy, alcohol and tobacco, was 2.6% in August. Food price inflation was 1.3%, unchanged from July. Trading Economics forecasts a September reading of about 3.4%, though that is only a forecast.
The figures matter because the Bank of England is due to decide on interest rates on 5 November, and markets are expecting a rise by the end of the year. Higher oil and energy prices could push inflation up.
levels.why: Inflation affects what households pay, and the figures will influence the Bank of England's next decision.

levels.headline: Next UK inflation figures due on 21 October
levels.body:
The ONS will release September's UK inflation figures on 21 October. For August, CPI inflation was 3.1%, CPIH was 3.3% and RPI was 3.4%.
Core inflation, which excludes food, energy, alcohol and tobacco, was 2.6%, and food inflation was 1.3%, the same as July. Trading Economics expects September to come in at about 3.4%, but this is a forecast only.
The Bank of England decides on rates on 5 November, and markets expect a rise by year end. Energy prices linked to the Iran conflict may add upward pressure on prices.
levels.why: The figures will shape expectations for interest rates and living costs.

levels.headline: UK inflation figures are due next week
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics will publish inflation for September on 21 October. In August, prices were rising at an annual rate of 3.1% by the main measure, CPI. Other measures were 3.3% (CPIH) and 3.4% (RPI).
Core inflation, without food, energy, alcohol and tobacco, was 2.6%. Food prices were rising by 1.3%, the same as in July. One forecaster expects September to be about 3.4%, but that is just a forecast.
The Bank of England will decide on interest rates on 5 November. Higher energy prices could push inflation up.
levels.why: Rising prices affect shopping bills and the decisions the Bank of England makes on interest rates.

levels.headline: September UK inflation figures due on 21 October
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics publishes September's UK inflation figures on 21 October. August's figure for CPI, the main measure, was 3.1%. CPIH was 3.3% and RPI was 3.4%.
Core inflation, which excludes food, energy, alcohol and tobacco, was 2.6%, and food inflation was 1.3%. One forecaster expects about 3.4% for September, though that is only a forecast.
The Bank of England next sets interest rates on 5 November, and the inflation figure will be watched closely.
levels.why: Inflation affects living costs and interest rates.

levels.headline: The next figures on how fast prices are rising are coming out next week
levels.body:
Every month, the Office for National Statistics says how much prices have gone up compared with a year ago. This is called inflation. The next figures come out on 21 October. They are for September.
In August prices were 3.1% higher than a year before. That means something that cost £100 now costs about £103. Food prices rose by less, 1.3%. One forecaster thinks September could be around 3.4%, but it is only a guess.
The Bank of England uses these numbers to help decide on interest rates, which it will do on 5 November.
levels.why: It tells us how fast prices in the shops are going up, and it affects interest rates.

levels.headline: New figures on rising prices come out next week
levels.body:
Each month, people count how much prices have gone up in a year. That is inflation. The next count comes out on 21 October.
In August, prices were 3.1% higher than a year before. So something that cost £100 now costs about £103. Food prices went up less, by 1.3%. One expert guesses that September may be about 3.4%.
The Bank of England uses these figures to help decide how high interest rates should be. It decides again on 5 November.
levels.why: It shows how much more things cost, and helps decide interest rates.

levels.headline: Next week we will learn how much prices have risen
levels.body:
Prices of things in shops usually go up a bit each year. This is called inflation. People count it every month. The next count is out on 21 October.
Last time it was 3.1%. That means something that cost £100 a year ago now costs about £103. Food went up less. An expert guesses it may be a bit higher this time.
The Bank of England uses it to decide on interest rates.
levels.why: It shows how much more things cost.

levels.headline: Counting how much more things cost
levels.body:
Do you remember when a bar of chocolate cost less? Prices tend to go up a little each year. Grown-ups count how much. That is called inflation.
The last count said prices went up by about 3 pence in every pound. The next count comes out on 21 October.
People who run the banks look at it to decide about interest, which is the extra money you pay for borrowing.
levels.why: It shows how much more things cost.

levels.headline: New figures show how fast prices are rising
levels.body:
Every month, people count how much more things cost than a year ago. This is called inflation. The next count comes out on 21 October.
In August it was 3.1%. That means something that cost £100 now costs about £103. Food went up by less.
The Bank of England uses the numbers to help decide on interest rates.
levels.why: It shows how much more things cost.

levels.headline: Pocket money and prices
levels.body:
Imagine your pocket money stays the same, but sweets cost a little more each year. Your money buys fewer sweets. Grown-ups count how much prices go up. They call it inflation.
The last count said prices went up a little, about 3 pence for every pound. The next count comes out on 21 October.
The people who look after the country's money watch it carefully.
levels.why: When prices go up, the same money buys less.
